blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Financial AI workflows that reuse investor knowledge need persistent memory that integrates observations across sources and periods without losing identity or provenance. In a knowledge graph, recurring observations may use different surface forms, fragmenting relationship histories and preventing evidence from accumulating. We introduce Fusion and Identity Registry for Memory Evolution (FIRME), a registry-anchored memory graph that reconciles incoming observations to persistent canonical relationships and retains their source, time, and context. Within periods, rule-based fusion links investor-call discussions to portfolio cash-flow signals, directly or through a fixed product-topic ontology. Across periods, canonical identities and persistent aliases direct recurring observations to the same relationship history; deterministic updates summarize reinforcement, inactivity, and reactivation. We evaluate FIRME on proprietary investor-call and cash-flow records and on S&P 500 earnings-call transcripts. Compared with a historical registry that retains canonical identities and semantic fallback but omits alias memory, FIRME increases final-period Correct Match Rate by 7.8-12.1 percentage points across four dataset-backend settings under a fixed-judge and fallback-review protocol. A blinded human audit of 200 incoming observations per setting finds Correct Match Rate gains of 9.0-16.5 points and reattachment-recall gains of 22.5-29.0 points, with higher observed merge precision in all four samples. A separate audit finds valid evidence paths for 293 of 300 outputs from full within-period fusion in the investor-call setting. Extraction-faithfulness and round-trip diagnostics assess source grounding and preservation of extractor-derived graph content.

blocks.en: 1. Introduction
blocks.zh: 1. 联合国 导言

blocks.en:
Understanding an investor’s interests requires attention to current evidence
and to how those interests and relationships change with market conditions.
The prominence of a concern such as market volatility may rise during
turbulence, recede as conditions stabilize, and return when uncertainty
increases. Reconstructing these trajectories therefore requires combining
heterogeneous sources of evidence. Unstructured text, including call records
and meeting notes, provides discussion context, whereas structured records,
such as financial-activity tables, capture measurable behavior. Because
interests can persist and return, past evidence should neither remain
permanently active nor disappear when observations are absent.
Agentic and tool-augmented financial workflows that reuse investor knowledge
depend on maintaining this knowledge across interactions. This requires
recurring observations to update the correct existing relationships while
retaining their supporting evidence.

blocks.en:
Maintaining evidence across sources and periods requires reconciliation.
Structured records and unstructured text differ in format and vocabulary;
the same entity or relationship can vary in name or phrasing over time.
Before entering the knowledge store, new evidence must therefore be aligned
across sources and matched to the correct persistent identity. Otherwise,
observations describing the same relationship form separate entities or
connections, each with a partial history, while cross-format supporting
evidence remains disconnected. Fragmented relationship histories in agent
memory can yield incomplete or redundant context for downstream reasoning
about an investor’s recurring concerns. Stable identity is necessary to accumulate
evidence under one persistent relationship and track its changes and
lifecycle over time.

blocks.en:
Temporal graph memories provide an important starting point. Zep/Graphiti
reconciles extracted entities with existing graph nodes, deduplicates facts,
links facts to source episodes, and represents when facts are valid or
invalidated; its evaluation emphasizes retrieval-supported question answering
and latency ( Rasmussen et al., 2025 ) . In the financial settings we study, the
central question is how evidence for the same relationship accumulates and
changes across periods. Incoming observations may use different names or come
from different sources, and some periods may contain no matched observation.
The graph-update challenge is to determine which relationship history
receives each new observation and how that relationship’s evidence strength
evolves with recurrence, inactivity, and renewed evidence.

blocks.en:
We introduce Fusion and Identity Registry for Memory Evolution (FIRME), a
knowledge graph (KG) memory framework, to address this challenge. A stable
head identifier anchors whose relationship is being tracked, while an evolving
registry reconciles target-name variants to canonical identities, anchoring
what that relationship concerns. Together, these identities determine which
persistent relationship history receives incoming evidence. The memory graph
retains each observation’s relation label, source, time, and context. When
conversational and structured evidence coexist, within-period fusion can
recognize their corroboration while preserving both observations. Across
periods, a recurring observation reinforces the corresponding history; periods
without matched observations lower its evidence strength while leaving earlier
evidence available. We test the incremental role of retained aliases against
a control that still uses historical canonical reconciliation and semantic
matching.

blocks.en:
Text-to-KG Construction and Canonicalization. Text-to-KG construction progressed from pattern-based extraction and
distant supervision ( Hearst, 1992 ; Mintz et al., 2009 ) to generative
relation extraction ( Josifoski et al., 2022 ) and LLM pipelines. LLM pipelines
add schema control and canonicalization: EDC separates open extraction,
schema definition, and canonicalization, while KGGen clusters related
entities ( Zhang and Soh, 2024 ; Mo et al., 2025 ) . GraphRAG structures extracted graphs
for corpus-level summarization ( Edge et al., 2024 ) , whereas open-KG methods
consolidate synonymous entity and relation
expressions ( Vashishth et al., 2018 ; Dash et al., 2021 ) . These approaches reduce
surface-form sparsity at construction time. They do not determine how
recurring observations drawn from heterogeneous sources should accumulate
under a single persistent relationship across successive time periods.

future facts from historical
representations ( Leblay and Chekol, 2018 ; Lacroix et al., 2020 ; Jin et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2021 ) .

FIRME’s central contribution is an identity-conditioned update of persistent
relationship histories across periods (Figure 1 ). Within-period
corroboration supports this update in paired investor-call data, while
lifecycle states make the resulting histories interpretable.

7.8–12.1 percentage points across four dataset–backend settings under the
judge and fallback-review protocol (Table 3 ). In the
shared blinded human audit (Table A2 ),
reattachment recall improves by 22.5–29.0 points, and observed merge

all entities of the same type in the prior registry R t − 1 R^{t-1} .

their canonical names and aliases. The system prompt for semantic
matching is provided in Appendix F.2 .

adopts the selected canonical ID, and its surface forms are added to that

We first evaluate whether registry-anchored reconciliation enables
recurring observations to accumulate under persistent relationship
identities. We define identity continuity as linking semantically equivalent
observations across periods to the same canonical relationship. We
compare RAW exact surface forms, spaCy-Lemma deterministic lemmatization ( Honnibal et al., 2020 ) , LLM-Norm independent within-period semantic normalization, FIRME w/o Alias Memory , and full FIRME .
LLM-Norm normalizes each period independently, after which equal
names or identifiers can be matched deterministically across periods.
To evaluate the incremental contribution of persistent alias memory,
we introduce FIRME w/o Alias Memory as a canonical-only historical
registry control. It retains canonical-ID and canonical-name matching
and cross-period semantic fallback, but removes the storage and reuse
of alternative names. Appendix B details
the control and the role of each comparison.

blocks.en: 4.3. Extraction Faithfulness

blocks.en:
Reliable memory accumulation requires not only cross-period identity
continuity but also source-grounded observations within each period.
We therefore assess extraction faithfulness through quotation
verification, entity traceability, and entity normalization.
Extraction faithfulness was evaluated on all final-period text-extracted
relationships produced by each extractor–backend configuration, before
fusion and cross-period reconciliation.
We trace four stages:
document, quoted evidence, raw entity mention, and normalized entity. Quotation Verification Rate is the share of extracted evidence
texts appearing in the source, flagging fabricated quotations. The Entity Traceability Rate measures the share of raw entity mentions
located in their associated evidence text using 0.7 token-overlap fuzzy
matching and a language-model fallback for paraphrases. Entity
Normalization Accuracy is the share of raw-to-normalized mappings judged
semantically correct. The Hallucination Rate is the proportion
of evaluated relationships whose evidence fails quotation verification
or whose raw target fails traceability. The Normalization Error Rate equals one minus normalization
accuracy. These diagnostics do not separately assess relation
entailment, direction, stance, or graph completeness. Because
verification and normalization are independent, verified edges may be
mismapped, while correctly mapped edges may contain hallucinated
evidence.

blocks.en: 4.4. Round-Trip Recovery

blocks.en:
An extractor may produce source-grounded outputs while still omitting
information from the input during extraction. Beyond extraction
faithfulness, we therefore evaluate preservation across representations.
Round-trip recovery measures how much extractor-derived
graph content survives graph-to-text generation and subsequent
re-extraction. Each reference graph contains the complete Opus 4.6
LLM2Graph output for one final-period call. For each corpus, we sampled
1,000 reference graphs uniformly with replacement and generated one
document for each sampled instance using a fixed Opus 4.6 generator.
These documents were shared across all evaluated re-extraction backends;
only the re-extraction backend varied. Because
generation may add document-grounded topics absent from the reference graph,
adjusted precision accepts an extra recovered item only when the fixed
Gemini 3.1 Pro judge determines that the document explicitly supports it.
We independently macro-average adjusted
precision, recall, and F1 across instances at node and edge levels.
Appendix H specifies node/edge matching and
the metric formulas.

Correct registry reattachments extend one cumulative evidence history rather
than create duplicate Emerging edges. FIRME’s higher

to the wrong anchor and history. Merge Precision therefore remains
important alongside CMR when assessing incorrect reattachments.

blocks.en: 6. Conclusion and Future Work
blocks.zh: 6. 结论和今后的工作

blocks.en:
We introduced FIRME, a registry-anchored memory-graph framework for
heterogeneous, time-varying investor evidence. Within-period ontology-mediated fusion
combines document-derived and structured evidence with provenance.
Cross-period registry reconciliation maps surface variants to canonical
relationships, allowing evidence to accumulate in one history through
deterministic lifecycle updates. Under the judge and fallback-review
protocol, FIRME increased CMR over the no-alias control by 7.8–12.1
percentage points and achieved 2.3–3.7 times LLM-Norm’s CMR.
The shared human audit found CMR gains of 9.0–16.5 points and
reattachment-recall gains of 22.5–29.0 points over the no-alias control,
with higher observed merge precision in all four samples. Results support persistent
identity for auditable evidence trajectories, not latent investor preference.

blocks.en: 7. Limitations
blocks.zh: 7. 限制

blocks.en:
FIRME’s lifecycle model is implemented as a deterministic state machine.
Given reconciliation decisions, its memory-strength score and lifecycle
state follow fixed, evidence-grounded updates; extraction and semantic
matching remain model-dependent.
The alias-memory ablation evaluates persistent aliases as a combined
mechanism, but does not separately quantify the effects of canonical
registry state and semantic fallback.

匹配仍然依赖模型。
别名-记忆衰竭评价了持久性化名的结合
机制,但不单独量化犬科动物
注册状态和语义倒置。

blocks.en:
The proprietary investor-call corpus and the internal product-annotation
resource underlying the ontology are not publicly available, limiting
independent reproduction of the corresponding experiments. The S&P 500 corpus
contains transcripts for 297 sampled companies across three reporting
periods but no paired structured cash-flow records. It therefore tests
extraction and temporal reconciliation, not the full heterogeneous-fusion
path. Neither window spans an annual cycle, limiting longer-term
seasonality and lifecycle conclusions.

Scoring : - 1.0: Same entity or concept . - 0.8 <= score < 1.0: Likely the same entity or concept . - 0.5 <= score < 0.8: Related but distinct . - 0.0 <= score < 0.5: Different meanings . blocks.en:
The review unit was an investor–product–period relationship, together with
its retained transcript evidence, structured cash-flow records, and any
cited product–topic ontology entry. Reviewers checked three aspects:
investor, product, and period alignment; source support for the discussion
and eligible cash-flow signal; and justification under the applicable fusion
rule. Rule 3 required discussion of the same product as the cash-flow signal.
Rule 4 required discussion of a topic appropriately associated with that
product in the frozen ontology. Direct outputs required a valid Rule 3 path;
Full outputs required at least one valid Rule 3 or Rule 4 path. Correctness
therefore concerned the evidence supporting the corroborated relationship.

投资者、产品和时期的调整;讨论的源支持
和符合资格的现金流动信号;以及适用聚变的理由
规则。 第3条要求讨论与现金流动信号相同的产品。
第4条要求讨论与《公约》
冷冻肿瘤中的产品 直接产出需要一条有效的规则3路径;
全部产出至少需要一条有效的规则3或规则4路径。 正确性
因此,涉及证明被证实的关系的证据。

blocks.en:
One disagreement concerned an investor–VTEB relationship. Annotator A judged
the corroboration correct because the topic discussion, ontology link to
VTEB, and eligible cash-flow signal aligned. Annotator B judged it incorrect
because the transcript did not directly mention VTEB. The annotators
revisited the evidence and Rule 4 criteria. Because Rule 4 permits
corroboration through a topic–product association, a direct product mention
was not required. The relationship was therefore resolved as correct.
This case illustrates how the rule criteria guided resolution of a disputed
judgment.
